items.title: Billy Taylor interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995
items.q: I mean he had Frank Wess, the tenor player, we were in the same band.

ctx.x: You know I want to ask you something about that. Because you know many of the musicians that we have interviewed have said the same thing. They said at some point early on in their careers, someone had faith in them and they said okay I’ll give you a chance. I’ll let you sit in. Or you meet that one person that you may be even intimidated by their status but they give you a chance. You know? And that’s wonderful. I’d like to see more of that in the school systems.

It’s happening. It doesn’t get the attention that it should because jazz doesn’t get the attention that it should. But it happened with me prior to getting to Virginia State. I was in high school at Delmar High School in Washington, D.C. and Henry Grant was the band director there. And he was just a wonderful band director. I mean he had Frank Wess, the tenor player, we were in the same band. As a matter of fact Frank is the reason I don’t play the tenor, because I figured if the tenor was supposed to sound like…

doing something wrong and I went back to the piano. Because he was a monster when he was just a teenager. I mean he was a wonderful player. And head and shoulders above most of us, you know. And so the — being in that context, I was lucky because not only did we have, did Frank and I have Henry Grant as a music teacher, we had James Reese Europe’s sister Mary Reese Europe, also on that faculty. Because of racial prejudice in Washington, D.C., this was an all-black school. We had five instructors with doctorates…

items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I used several flutes to get the four flute sound I had to go through Jerome Richardson and Herby Man and Frank Wess and several other guys to complete the dates.

ctx.x: The pianist who played the wonderful introduction to “Body and Soul” with Coleman Hawkins. This was a huge guy and I am going to think of everybody’s name as soon as I get off mike. I can’t think of his name either. But he brought a trio into the composer when I worked there. So I am looking at this… listening to this guy. He has got Tommy Williams and this other gentleman who is a wonderful drummer. I still can’t think of the piano player’s name though. So the drummer’s… thank you very much… the drummer’s name…

flutes going all the way from piccolo down to the bass flute. And it was a wonderful sound. I said, “Now you tell me. Why didn’t you tell me this before I made my record?” He laughed. He said, “That’s why I wanted you on the record because I knew you liked to play in this context. But man he had scored something… I wish… one of these days maybe I will go back and do that material with that combination because it was just a beautiful… it was a wonderful commercial. Whatever the syrup was or whatever the chocolate…

items.title: Frank Wess — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I don’t have any connection with Washington other than Billy Taylor, you know?

ctx.x: Ken was just saying Ron Carter was there.
Oh he was there? I didn’t hear about it. I don’t have any connection with Washington other than Billy Taylor, you know? He’s so different, you know? To me, nothing is ever quite right. It's close.

items.title: Frank Wess interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995
items.q: My teacher, Henry L. Grant, who was also Duke Ellington’s teacher and Billy Taylor, Dr. Billy Taylor and I studied with him.

ctx.x: What led you to pick up that instrument as a jazz horn?

Oh well that started years ago when I was in high school. My teacher, Henry L. Grant, who was also Duke Ellington’s teacher and Billy Taylor, Dr. Billy Taylor and I studied with him. And he was the orchestra teacher you know. And he gave me a flute to take home you know. So I took it home and after fooling with it a while I realized that I couldn’t do it without a teacher, you know. And at the time, you know I couldn’t afford a teacher and there wasn’t one available that I knew of. So I said I’ll just let it rest…

was looking for a tenor player you know, so he kept calling and calling. He called for a couple of years and I told him I was doing something, you know, and I couldn’t leave right then. So he just kept calling. Periodically he would call. And in the meantime I got a degree, a bachelor’s degree in flute, and we got together and I joined Basie. Well the thing was at the time I mean, what made me go with him because actually I had quit the road five years before I joined Basie. You know I’d given up on the road…
